title: YOU CAN TRUST GOD AND STILL HATE WHAT THIS SEASON FEELS LIKE.
paragraphs: YOU CAN TRUST GOD AND STILL HATE WHAT THIS SEASON FEELS LIKE.

You are not losing your faith just because you are tired of the pain. Psalm 13 reveals something many suffering Christians desperately need to hear: God never demanded that you pretend your heart wasn't breaking in order to prove that you still believe in Him.
There is a kind of suffering that doesn't make you stop believing in God.
It just makes you wonder how much longer you can keep believing while hurting this badly.
And that is the part nobody sees.
They see you at church. They see you sharing Scripture. They see you encouraging someone else not to give up. They see you bowing your head when someone prays.
But they don't see what happens when you get home.
When the door closes.
When the distractions disappear.
When you finally sit on the edge of your bed, stare at the floor, and realize you have spent another entire day trying to be strong while something inside you is quietly falling apart.
You still believe God is good.
You just don't understand why life feels this cruel.
You still believe He hears prayer.
You just wonder why the prayer you have repeated a hundred times seems to have changed nothing.
You still believe He has a purpose.
You just wish the purpose didn't hurt so much.
And somewhere in the middle of that exhaustion, another painful thought begins whispering:
Maybe a stronger Christian wouldn't feel this way.
Maybe someone with more faith would stop crying.
Maybe someone who really trusted God wouldn't feel disappointed.
Maybe you should be grateful instead of grieving.
Maybe admitting how badly this season hurts means you are questioning the very God you claim to love.
But what if that guilt is coming from something God never actually required of you?
What if you have confused trusting God with pretending suffering doesn't hurt?
And what if one of the most honest prayers in the entire Bible was written by a man who loved God deeply, yet felt as though God had forgotten him?
Before you condemn yourself for struggling, you need to hear what David dared to say.
Because Psalm 13 may change the way you understand faith in the middle of suffering.
David begins with words that sound almost too painful to belong in Scripture.
"How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" — Psalm 13:1 (KJV)
Read that again.
This was not an unbeliever mocking God.
This was David.
A man whose life was marked by God's calling, God's mercy, God's deliverance, and God's covenant promises.
Yet here he was, asking whether the Lord had forgotten him.
In the original Hebrew, the cry begins:
עַד־אָנָה יְהוָה
ʿAd-ʾānâ YHWH
"How long, O LORD?"
The expression ʿad-ʾānâ carries the question of duration. How long will this continue? How much longer must this be endured?
And David doesn't ask it once.
He repeats the cry four times in the opening two verses.
How long?
How long?
How long?
How long?
The repetition matters.
It is the sound of a heart that has reached the point where the length of suffering has become part of the suffering itself.
There are wounds that hurt because of what happened.
And there are wounds that hurt because of how long nothing has changed.
You can endure something for a week while telling yourself that relief is coming.
You can survive a difficult month by believing things will soon improve.
But what happens when the weeks become months?
When the months become years?
When you have prayed, waited, obeyed, forgiven, endured, and tried to remain faithful, yet the burden is still there?
What happens when you are not only exhausted by what you are facing, but exhausted by how long you have been facing it?
David knew something about that.
And God, in His wisdom, preserved David's painful questions in Holy Scripture.
Not because every conclusion a suffering person reaches about God is necessarily correct.
But because God has given His people words with which to bring their anguish honestly before Him.
David felt forgotten.
That does not mean God had forgotten him.
David felt that God's face was hidden.
That does not mean God had abandoned His covenant faithfulness.
There is a difference between what suffering makes us feel and what God's character assures us is true.
And biblical faith learns to bring those two realities into the same prayer.
That distinction may be exactly what you need today.
Because perhaps you have been treating your emotions as evidence against your faith.
You wake up anxious, so you assume you aren't trusting enough.
You cry again, so you assume you haven't surrendered enough.
You feel discouraged, so you wonder whether your relationship with God is failing.
But Scripture does not teach that every faithful believer will experience emotional peace at every moment.
It teaches us where to turn when peace feels painfully distant.
David continues:
"How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" — Psalm 13:2 (KJV)
There is something painfully familiar about that phrase.
Having sorrow in my heart daily.
Not occasionally.
Not only when something terrible happens.
Daily.
The kind of sorrow that follows you into ordinary moments.
You wash dishes with it.
You drive to work with it.
You sit through meetings with it.
You answer messages with it.
You laugh at something funny, and for a moment you almost forget.
Then the memory returns.
The diagnosis.
The betrayal.
The empty chair.
The unanswered prayer.
The debt.
The marriage that feels colder every month.
The child you cannot reach.
The future that looks nothing like what you imagined when you first prayed for it.
And sometimes the hardest part is that everyone else seems to be moving forward while you are still trying to survive something they think you should have overcome by now.
You hear testimonies about breakthroughs.
You celebrate someone else's answered prayer.
You sincerely thank God for blessing them.
But later, alone, you whisper something you would never dare say in a crowded church:
Lord, when will it be my turn?
And then you feel guilty for even asking.
But listen carefully.
David's question did not disqualify his prayer.
It became part of his prayer.
That is the beauty of biblical lament.
Lament is not simply complaining about life.
It is bringing grief, confusion, fear, and painful questions before God while continuing to address Him as the One who hears.
It is sorrow directed toward the Lord rather than away from Him.
It does not require you to deny what hurts.
And it does not require you to declare that everything God permits is pleasant.
The Bible calls death an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26).
It tells believers to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15).
It describes Jesus Himself as a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3).
There are things in this fallen world that are genuinely heartbreaking.
Sin is destructive.
Death is grievous.
Betrayal is painful.
Injustice is evil.
Loss is real.
And Christians do not glorify God by pretending otherwise.
Sometimes we glorify Him by refusing to let our pain become the final authority over what we believe about Him.
That does not mean we never struggle.
It means we keep bringing the struggle into His presence.
Perhaps that is what you have been missing.
You thought faith meant never asking why.
But David asked how long.
You thought faith meant never feeling overwhelmed.
But David spoke of daily sorrow.
You thought faith meant never being afraid.
But David pleaded for God to intervene before his enemies could rejoice over his downfall.
And God did not erase those words from the Bible.
He preserved them for generations of suffering believers.
Including you.
There is another Hebrew expression in Psalm 13 that deserves our attention.
When David asks why God hides His face, the Hebrew reads:
תַּסְתִּיר אֶת־פָּנֶיךָ מִמֶּנִּי
Tastîr ʾet-pāneykā mimmennî.
"You hide Your face from me."
In the biblical world, the imagery of God's face is deeply connected to His favorable attention and presence.
Think about the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:25:
"The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee."
David's anguish is not merely that his circumstances are difficult.
He longs to experience the favor and nearness of the God he loves.
And isn't that sometimes the deepest wound of all?
Not merely that life is painful.
But that God feels distant while life is painful.
You can survive many things when you sense that someone is beside you.
But when heaven seems silent, even ordinary burdens can feel unbearable.
Still, we must be careful.
The feeling of divine distance is not proof of divine absence.
Psalm 13 gives us David's honest experience, not a declaration that God had ceased caring for him.
And this matters because suffering can distort our perception.
Pain can make silence feel like rejection.
Delay can feel like indifference.
Unanswered questions can feel like abandonment.
But God's faithfulness is not measured by how clearly we can perceive His presence on a particular day.
Sometimes faith must rest upon what God has revealed when our emotions cannot confirm it.
And this is where the psalm begins to turn.
Not because David suddenly receives everything he has been asking for.
Not because the enemy disappears.
Not because the circumstances are reported to have changed.
But because David takes his anguish directly to God.
"Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death." — Psalm 13:3 (KJV)
Notice those words.
O LORD my God.
David has just described feeling forgotten.
He has spoken of daily sorrow.
He has asked why God seems hidden.
Yet he still says:
My God.
That little word changes everything.
Not because it erases the pain.
But because it reveals that David's pain has not severed his relationship with the Lord.
He does not say, "I understand everything."
He does not say, "This no longer hurts."
He does not say, "I finally see why all of this happened."
He says, in effect:
God, I am suffering, and I am still coming to You.
There is a profound difference between bringing your questions to God and deciding that your questions make God unworthy of trust.
One is the language of lament.
The other can become a rejection of the One who alone can ultimately redeem us.
And if you are still praying, even weakly, even tearfully, even with words you can barely form, do not despise that prayer because it does not sound victorious.
A trembling prayer can still be an act of faith.
A tearful confession can still be sincere worship.
A believer who whispers, "Lord, help me," has not failed simply because those are the only words left.
Remember the father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
Jesus did not require him to pretend his struggle was nonexistent.
The father brought both his belief and his need for help to Christ.
And perhaps you need permission to pray with that kind of honesty.
Not permission to accuse God falsely.
Not permission to justify bitterness or rebellion.
But permission to stop performing emotional strength you do not possess.
You do not need to manufacture a smile before approaching the throne of grace.
You need a Savior.
And that brings us to something even more extraordinary than David's lament.
Because Psalm 13 is not the only place Scripture reveals the anguish of someone who truly trusts God.
Centuries later, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus Christ faced suffering beyond anything we can fully comprehend.
Matthew 26:38 records His words:
"My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death."
Think about that.
Jesus was perfectly sinless.
Perfectly obedient.
Perfectly united in will with His Father.
Yet He described His soul as overwhelmed with sorrow.
He did not call the approaching agony pleasant.
He did not pretend that the cross would be painless.
He prayed:
"O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." — Matthew 26:39 (KJV)
In the Greek text, the phrase translated "exceeding sorrowful" includes the word:
περίλυπος
Perilypos.
Deeply grieved. Overwhelmed with sorrow.
The Gospels do not present Jesus as emotionally untouched by suffering.
They reveal the true humanity of the Son of God, who faced the horror before Him with real anguish and perfect obedience.
And here is the distinction we cannot afford to miss.
Surrender does not mean suffering stops feeling painful.
Jesus submitted to the Father's will while honestly expressing the anguish of what lay ahead.
His obedience was not made less perfect by His sorrow.
And while our suffering is not identical to His unique, saving sacrifice, His example destroys the idea that painful emotions automatically prove spiritual failure.
There is no sin in grieving what is genuinely grievous.
There is no spiritual achievement in calling evil good.
There is no biblical requirement to enjoy the breaking of your heart.
But there is an invitation to entrust your heart to the One who suffered for sinners and conquered the grave.
And the story becomes even more breathtaking at Calvary.
As Jesus hung upon the cross, He cried:
"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" — Matthew 27:46 (KJV)
The words recorded in Matthew are:
Ἠλί, Ἠλί, λεμὰ σαβαχθανί
Ēli, Ēli, lema sabachthani.
Matthew preserves this Semitic cry, reflecting the language spoken in Jesus' world, and supplies its Greek meaning.
These words deliberately echo Psalm 22:1.
Jesus was not merely expressing ordinary frustration.
He was enduring the suffering of the cross as the sinless Messiah who gave Himself for our redemption.
Christ's cry must be understood within His unique saving work, not reduced to the experience of an ordinary believer having a difficult season.
Yet the connection remains profoundly comforting.
The Savior who calls us to trust Him is not a stranger to anguish.
He knows what it means to suffer.
He knows what it means to be rejected.
He knows the reality of tears, betrayal, cruelty, and death.
And because He rose again, suffering and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why Christian hope is more than positive thinking.
It is anchored in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
The cross does not tell you that your pain is imaginary.
It tells you that God has acted decisively to redeem sinners through the suffering of His Son.
The empty tomb does not promise that every earthly circumstance will improve according to your preferred timetable.
It declares that Jesus has defeated death and that His people have a living hope.
And that hope can sustain you even when this season remains terribly difficult.
Now return to David.
Because the ending of Psalm 13 is one of the most beautiful movements of faith in Scripture.
After the questions.
After the sorrow.
After the desperate plea for help.
David says:
"But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." — Psalm 13:5 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the opening phrase is:
וַאֲנִי בְּחַסְדְּךָ בָטַחְתִּי
Vaʾanî beḥasdekā bāṭaḥtî.
"But I have trusted in Your steadfast love."
The Hebrew word חֶסֶד (ḥesed) is especially important.
It speaks of loyal love, covenant faithfulness, and mercy. Its meaning depends on context, and no single English word captures every shade of it.
David's confidence is not grounded in a sudden change of emotion.
It is grounded in the faithful character of God.
Notice what the psalm does not say.
It does not tell us that David's enemies disappeared before he began to praise.
It does not tell us that every troubling question was answered.
It does not tell us that all his sorrow instantly vanished.
Instead, David moves from lament to trust by remembering who God is.
He does not deny the reality of his pain.
He refuses to let pain have the final word about God's faithfulness.
And perhaps that is what trusting God will look like for you today.
Not a dramatic breakthrough.
Not an immediate answer.
Not waking up tomorrow with every burden removed.
Perhaps it will look like opening your Bible even though you are still hurting.
Perhaps it will look like asking a trusted believer to pray with you because you cannot carry this alone.
Perhaps it will look like seeking wise pastoral care or professional help when your suffering has become overwhelming.
Perhaps it will look like confessing resentment you have allowed to grow, while also acknowledging that your grief itself is not something you must pretend away.
Perhaps it will look like telling God:
Father, I don't like this.
I don't understand it.
I wish things were different.
I am tired of waiting.
But I still need You.
I still believe Jesus is my Savior.
And I am asking You to help me trust You through what I cannot change.
That is not polished religious language.
It is a heart learning to lament faithfully.
And there is something else you must understand.
You can trust God's sovereignty without claiming to know the specific reason behind every tragedy.
Romans 8:28 assures believers that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
But the next verse shows us something essential about that good.
Romans 8:29 speaks of being conformed to the image of His Son.
God's promise is not that every event will feel good.
Nor that every loss will be reversed in this life.
Nor that every prayer will receive the answer we desire.
His purpose reaches deeper than temporary comfort.
He is conforming His people to Christ, and His saving work will culminate in glory.
That does not make every painful experience good in itself.
It means evil, suffering, and loss cannot ultimately overthrow God's redemptive purposes.
And sometimes the most faithful words you can say are simply:
I do not know why this happened.
But I know who Jesus is.
There are believers who have buried people they desperately prayed would live.
There are Christians who have remained faithful through years of illness.
There are parents who continue praying for children who seem farther from God than ever.
There are husbands and wives who have done everything they know to do and still live with grief.
There are people reading this right now who are trying to rebuild after a decision they deeply regret.
And others who are suffering because of someone else's sin.
Not every wound has the same cause.
Not every painful season is divine discipline.
Not every hardship is punishment for a hidden sin.
Jesus Himself challenged simplistic assumptions about suffering in John 9:1–3.
So please do not allow someone to explain your entire life with a careless sentence.
"You must not have enough faith."
"You should be over it by now."
"If you really trusted God, you wouldn't be sad."
Those statements can crush people whom Scripture calls us to comfort.
And if you have ever said something like that to a suffering believer, there is grace for you too.
Repent.
Learn to listen.
Learn to weep with those who weep.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can offer someone is not an explanation.
It is compassionate presence, truthful encouragement, and a willingness to remain beside them when there is no quick solution.
That is part of bearing one another's burdens, as Galatians 6:2 commands.
And perhaps this is why your story matters more than you realize.
Not because every suffering person must turn their pain into public testimony.
You are allowed to grieve privately.
You are allowed to heal without making your wounds an exhibition.
But when you are ready, your honest testimony may remind another believer that they are not alone.
Someone needs to hear that you still love Jesus even though life has been difficult.
Someone needs to know that you cried and prayed in the same night.
Someone needs to see that trusting Christ does not require pretending everything is fine.
Someone may have been silently drowning beneath the expectation that Christians must always appear joyful.
And your honesty, grounded in God's Word, could help them bring their own pain to the Lord.
This is why I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a test of how spiritual you are.
Not because your answer needs to impress anyone.
But because there may be someone reading the comments who needs to discover that another believer understands.
What has been the hardest part of trusting God in this season of your life?
Is it the waiting?
The silence?
The disappointment?
The loneliness?
The fear that things may never return to what they were?
Or, if you need your brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, write:
You do not have to reveal details you are not ready to share.
But do not believe the lie that you are the only Christian who has ever struggled this deeply.
And if you see someone asking for prayer, consider taking a moment to pray for them sincerely.
Not merely reacting to their pain.
Not rushing to correct their emotions.
But remembering that behind those words is a real person, carrying a real burden, who needs the grace and comfort of Christ.
That is what Christian community should look like.
Not a gathering of people competing to appear strong.
But a family of redeemed sinners learning to walk in truth, repentance, compassion, and hope.
And that is also why the work of Gospel Warrior matters to us.
We believe biblical encouragement should do more than give someone a temporary emotional lift.
It should lead them back to Scripture.
Back to sound doctrine.
Back to prayer.
Back to repentance where repentance is needed.
Back to the grace of Jesus Christ.
Back to a deeper understanding of the Gospel that can sustain them when inspiration fades and suffering remains.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers move beyond merely surviving from one encouraging post to the next.
We want people to become rooted in the Word.
To recognize error.
To understand grace.
To grow in holiness.
To learn how to suffer faithfully.
To become more like Jesus.
Not because giving money earns His favor.
It never could.
It should not.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
What it can do is help sustain and expand this work.
It can help us continue developing Christian resources.
It can help make more biblical teaching available.
It can help this message reach another weary believer who may be struggling to find the words to pray.
These products are simply an added expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
Helping people know Jesus.
Helping believers become grounded in Scripture.
Helping wounded hearts encounter the truth of God's grace.
Helping people discover that their failures do not have to become the final chapter of their story.
You are no less welcome.
You are no less valuable.
Your financial situation does not determine your standing before God or your place in this community.
You can still help by praying, engaging thoughtfully, and sharing biblical encouragement with people who need it.
Someone who has stopped telling people how much they are hurting.
Someone who thinks their tears make them a bad Christian.
Someone who has been avoiding prayer because they feel ashamed of their questions.
Someone who needs to open Psalm 13 tonight and realize that God has given His children language for sorrow.
If a particular person comes to mind, consider tagging them with kindness, or sending this privately if their situation is sensitive.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually cold, and even those who do not yet know Christ.
Not merely to grow a page.
But because the message of Jesus Christ is too important to be buried beneath the noise of everything else.
And now, before you leave, there is one more verse in Psalm 13 that I do not want you to miss.
The final verse.
"I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me." — Psalm 13:6 (KJV)
What an ending.
David began by asking whether God had forgotten him.
He ends by remembering God's goodness.
He began with anguish.
He ends with worship.
But notice something beautiful.
The psalm never explicitly tells us that his outward circumstances changed.
That is important.

Because sometimes we read testimonies and assume every faithful story must end with the sickness healed, the marriage restored, the money provided, the relationship repaired, or the long-awaited answer finally arriving.
Sometimes God graciously grants those things.
Sometimes He does not.
And His goodness does not depend on our receiving every earthly outcome we desire.
David's song is not a guarantee that every painful situation will end the way we hope.
It is a testimony that God's steadfast love remains worthy of trust.
That is the kind of faith we need.
Not a faith that collapses whenever life becomes difficult.
Not a faith that refuses to acknowledge grief.
Not a faith that treats tears as disobedience.
But a faith anchored in the God who has revealed His mercy through Jesus Christ.
A faith that can mourn without surrendering hope.
A faith that can ask questions without abandoning prayer.
A faith that can repent when suffering exposes sin, yet refuse to mistake every painful emotion for sin.
A faith that understands that God's ultimate promise is not a trouble-free earthly life, but eternal life through His Son.
And if you are reading this while carrying a burden you have not told anyone about, I want you to remember something.
You do not need to solve the mystery of your suffering tonight.
You do not need to explain why God allowed every painful chapter.
You do not need to predict when your circumstances will change.
You do not need to force yourself to feel happy about what has broken your heart.
But you can come to Jesus.
You can confess your sins and receive His mercy.
You can bring Him your sorrow.
You can ask Him for wisdom, endurance, and help.
You can trust His promises even when your feelings are unsettled.
And you can remember that the same Savior who died for sinners rose again and now intercedes for those who belong to Him.
Hebrews 4:15–16 reminds us that we have a High Priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses and invites us to approach the throne of grace for mercy and help in time of need.
Not after we have become emotionally impressive.
Not after we have stopped crying.
Not after we have found all the answers.
In our time of need.
That includes tonight.
That includes this difficult season.
That includes the moment when you are so tired that all you can whisper is:
Jesus, please help me.
And perhaps, right there, your next step of faith begins.
Not with a triumphant declaration that everything is wonderful.
But with the simple decision to bring your wounded heart to the Lord who is faithful.
Because the Christian life is not a story about how strong we managed to become.
It is a story about the grace of God in Jesus Christ, who saves sinners and sustains His people.
It is a story of repentance and forgiveness.
Of mercy for the undeserving.
Of redemption that cannot be purchased.
Of hope that reaches beyond the grave.
Of a Savior who is not ashamed to call His redeemed people His brothers and sisters.
And for those who have wandered far from Him, the invitation is still to repent and believe the Gospel.
Your failures may have consequences.
Your choices may have left painful scars.
Your story may contain chapters you wish you could erase.
But forgiveness and new life are found in Jesus Christ.
That is why our message has never been merely about feeling better.
It is about being reconciled to God.
It is about being transformed by grace.
It is about the Lord who can redeem what sin has devastated and give His people a future that death itself cannot destroy.
So if this season hurts, tell Him.
If you are afraid, tell Him.
If you are disappointed, tell Him.
If you are tired, tell Him.
And when you cannot find the strength to sing, you can still pray.
When you cannot understand His providence, you can still hold to His promises.
When you cannot see what tomorrow holds, you can still remember the One who rose from the dead.
You may not love what this season feels like.
You may not understand why it has lasted so long.
You may still have questions when you finish reading this.
But you do not have to pretend your pain is pleasant to trust the God who is faithful.
You can hate what this season feels like without hating the God who is holding you through it.
And perhaps one day, when you look back, you will not remember this as the season when you finally learned how to stop crying.
Perhaps you will remember it as the season when you learned that even through your tears, you could keep coming to Jesus.
Because the goal was never to become a person who could no longer be wounded.
The goal is to belong to Christ, trust His Word, and be transformed by His grace.
And the God who began a good work in His people will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).
So tonight, you may still be in Psalm 13's opening words.
How long, O LORD?
You may not yet feel ready to sing the final verse.
But you can still bring your heart to the same faithful God.
And that is where this story leaves us.
Not with every question answered.
Not with every tear dried.
But with our eyes turned toward Jesus Christ, our crucified and risen Savior, in whom God's promises find their fulfillment.
Your tears do not have to stop before your heart can turn toward the One who will one day wipe them all away.
